sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Senior and staff-level Go interviews always include engineering practices questions. Interviewers want to know how you raise the quality of code your team writes, how you make architectural decisions visible and reversible, and how you coach less-experienced engineers. This module is about demonstrating technical leadership in the context of idiomatic Go—not just 'best practices' in the abstract, but the specific conventions and tools the Go community has converged on.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Technical leadership in a Go codebase operates at three levels: (1) Code level — code review guidelines, golangci-lint configuration, idiomatic patterns (error wrapping with %w, table-driven tests, interface segregation). (2) Design level — ADRs for significant decisions (choosing a web framework, adopting generics, selecting a DB library), reviewed as PRs so they are versioned. (3) Team level — onboarding material for Go idioms, mentoring through pair programming on real issues (debugging a race condition, optimising a hot path), fostering psychological safety in code review.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. Code review for Go: check for unchecked errors, naked returns, exported functions without doc comments, unnecessary pointer receivers, improper use of init(). 2. Technical debt in Go: identify by measuring cyclomatic complexity (gocyclo), lack of interface boundaries, global state, missing test coverage. 3. ADRs: lightweight decision record (title, status, context, decision, consequences); stored in /docs/adr as Markdown; reviewed as a PR. 4. Idiomatic Go standards: Effective Go, Go Code Review Comments, Google Go Style Guide; enforce via golangci-lint .golangci.yml committed to repo. 5. Mentoring Go: identify common beginner mistakes (goroutine leaks, error ignored with _, over-use of interface{}), design focused exercises, give specific actionable code-review comments with links to Effective Go.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: • 'How do you maintain code quality in a fast-moving Go team?' → golangci-lint in CI as a hard gate, code review checklist, ADRs for big decisions, weekly Go idiom sharing. • 'How would you manage technical debt in a large Go codebase?' → inventory with gocyclo/coverage metrics, classify as hygiene vs. structural, allocate 20% of sprint capacity, track as regular issues. • 'What makes a good Go code review?' → check for unchecked errors, verify interfaces are minimal, confirm context propagation, validate error messages are lowercase without punctuation, check test coverage of new code. • 'How do you write an ADR for a Go library choice?' → context section explains what problem we're solving, decision section names the library with reasoning, consequences list trade-offs including transitive deps and maintenance risk.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "When I join a Go team, one of the first things I do is check whether golangci-lint is in CI and whether there is a committed .golangci.yml. If not, I propose adding one with a conservative initial ruleset—staticcheck, errcheck, govet—so we don't break everyone at once, then gradually enable more linters as issues are fixed. For code reviews I focus on three Go-specific things that automated tools miss: whether context is propagated correctly through the call stack, whether error messages follow Go conventions (lowercase, no period), and whether newly introduced interfaces are the minimal set the consumer actually needs. For architectural decisions I introduce ADRs as a Markdown PR: the team discusses in the PR comments, we record the decision, and future engineers can read the history of why we made a choice rather than just what the choice was. For mentoring I pair on real production issues—there is no better way to teach goroutine lifecycle than debugging an actual leak together."
